title: Home & everyday objects
goal: Name rooms and household objects, say where things are, and say what there is and isn't.
intro:
A traditional Pashtun house (کور) is built around a walled **courtyard** (انګړ), with rooms opening onto it and a flat roof (بام) where people sleep on summer nights. Many villages also have a **حجره** (hujrá), the men's guest house where visitors are received.

In this unit you'll learn household words and the Pashto way of saying 'in', 'on', 'under', 'near': not just prepositions (before the noun) or postpositions (after it) but often **both at once** — په کوټه کې 'in the room', literally 'in room in'.

vocab.note: m · pl: کورونه korúna. کور ته 'home(wards)'.

vocab.en: in (after the noun, with په before it)

vocab.note: په مېز باندې or پر مېز 'on the table'.

phrases.en: The key is on the table.
Turn the fan on, it's hot.

phrases.native: ماشومان په انګړ کې لوبې کوي.
phrases.roman: māshumā́n pə angáṛ ke lóbe kawí.
phrases.en: The children are playing in the courtyard.

grammar.title: In, on, under, near: adpositions that wrap around the noun
grammar.body:
Pashto location words often come in two parts, one **before** and one **after** the noun (a *circumposition*). The noun in the middle is in the oblique case — for many singular nouns this looks the same as the basic form, but feminine -a nouns change to -e after د (د دروازې).

په … کې pə … ke — in
په … باندې pə … bā́nde (or پر … pər …) — on
د … لاندې də … lā́nde — under
د … څنګ ته də … tsang ta — beside
د … شا ته də … shā ta — behind
د … مخې ته də … mə́xe ta — in front of
… ته نږدې … ta nəẓdé — near

The first parts (په، د، پر) are *prepositions*; the second parts (کې، باندې، لاندې، ته) are *postpositions*. Some words, like کې and ته, can't be used without their partner. In casual speech, people often drop په and just say کور کې 'at home'.

examples.en: The child is in the room.
The cup is on the table.
The cat is under the bed.

examples.native: موټر د کور شا ته دی.
examples.roman: moṭár də kor shā ta day.
examples.en: The car is behind the house.

examples.native: زموږ کور جومات ته نږدې دی.
examples.roman: zmuẓ kor jumā́t ta nəẓdé day.
examples.en: Our house is near the mosque.

examples.native: د دروازې څنګ ته يوه څوکۍ ده.
examples.roman: də darwā́ze tsang ta yáwa tsawkə́y da.
examples.en: There's a chair beside the door.

grammar.title: 'There is / there isn't': شته and نشته
grammar.body:
**شته** (shta) means 'there is / there are / exists' and **نشته** (nə́shta) 'there isn't / there aren't'. They never change for gender or number, which makes them very handy: چای شته 'there's tea', اوبه نشته 'there's no water'.

To say where something is, you can also use the ordinary copula دی / ده / دي after a location: په کوټه کې يو کټ **دی** 'in the room there is a bed'. شته stresses existence or availability (especially in questions and answers: ... شته؟ – هو، شته / نه، نشته), while دی/ده simply locates the thing.

examples.en: Is there any milk in the fridge?

examples.native: په دې کوټه کې دوه کړکۍ دي.
examples.roman: pə de kóṭa ke dwa kaṛkə́y di.
examples.en: There are two windows in this room.

examples.native: زموږ په کلي کې روغتون نشته.
examples.roman: zmuẓ pə kə́li ke roġtún nə́shta.
examples.en: There's no hospital in our village.

dialogue.title: Showing a guest the room
dialogue.setting: Shah Mahmood welcomes his friend's cousin, Asad, who is staying the night.

lines.speaker: Shah Mahmood
lines.native: په خير راغلې! راشه، دننه راشه.
lines.roman: pə xayr rā́ġle! rā́sha, danə́na rā́sha.

lines.speaker: Asad
lines.en: Thanks. Where shall I take my shoes off?

lines.speaker: Shah Mahmood
lines.native: دلته، د دروازې څنګ ته. دا ستا کوټه ده.
lines.roman: dálta, də darwā́ze tsang ta. dā stā kóṭa da.
lines.en: Here, beside the door. This is your room.

lines.speaker: Asad
lines.native: ډېره ښکلې کوټه ده! تشناب چېرته دی؟
lines.roman: ḍéra ṣkə́le kóṭa da! tashnā́b chérta day?
lines.en: It's a lovely room! Where's the bathroom?

lines.speaker: Shah Mahmood
lines.native: تشناب هلته دی، د انګړ په بل سر کې.
lines.roman: tashnā́b hálta day, də angáṛ pə bəl sar ke.
lines.en: The bathroom is over there, at the other end of the courtyard.

lines.speaker: Asad
lines.native: په کوټه کې پکه شته؟ ډېره ګرمي ده.
lines.roman: pə kóṭa ke páka shta? ḍéra garmí da.
lines.en: Is there a fan in the room? It's very hot.

lines.speaker: Shah Mahmood
lines.native: هو، شته، خو اوس برېښنا نشته. د شپې بام ته ځو.
lines.roman: ho, shta, xo os breṣnā́ nə́shta. də shpe bām ta dzu.
lines.en: Yes, there is, but there's no electricity right now. At night we go up to the roof.

lines.speaker: Asad
lines.native: ښه، سمه ده. اوبه چېرته دي؟
lines.roman: ṣə, sáma da. obə́ chérta di?

lines.speaker: Shah Mahmood
lines.native: په پخلنځي کې، په يخچال کې. ګيلاس په مېز باندې دی.
lines.roman: pə paxlandzí ke, pə yaxchā́l ke. gilā́s pə mez bā́nde day.
lines.en: In the kitchen, in the fridge. There's a glass on the table.

lines.speaker: Asad
lines.en: Thanks very much — bless your home!

culture: Shoes come off at the door of a room with carpets, and guests are given the best place to sit — often cushions (توشکې) along the walls of the guest room. In many Pashtun homes the women's quarters are private, so a male visitor is received in the guest room or the village **حجره**, where men gather in the evenings to talk, drink tea and settle local matters. Power cuts (لوډشېډنګ in Pakistan) are common in both countries, so people sleep in the courtyard or on the roof in summer.
